items.title: 3.4.1 Rational Equations Reducible to the Quadratic Equation

blocks.text: A rational equation is an equation containing one or more rational expressions, where the rational expressions usually have the variable in the denominator.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A rational expression is a fraction whose numerator and denominator are polynomials, for example \(\frac{1}{x}\), \(\frac{2}{x+1}\) or \(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\).
Because division by zero is not defined, every value of \(x\) that makes a denominator zero is excluded. That is why the book writes conditions such as \(x \ne 0, x \ne -1\) next to the equation: these values can never be solutions.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Method for a rational equation:
1. Write the excluded values (denominator \(= 0\)).
2. Find the LCD of all the denominators.
3. Multiply EVERY term on both sides by the LCD; the fractions disappear.
4. Expand, bring all terms to one side and get \(ax^{2} + bx + c = 0\).
5. Solve (factorisation or the quadratic formula).
6. Reject any root that is an excluded value, and check the rest in the original equation.

blocks.title: Example 7
steps:
Given: \(\dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{2}{x+1} = 1\), with \(x \ne 0\) and \(x \ne -1\).
To find: all values of \(x\) that satisfy the equation (the solution set).
Method: the variable is in two denominators, so this is a rational equation. Multiply both sides by the LCD \(x(x+1)\) to clear the fractions, rearrange into \(ax^{2} + bx + c = 0\), and solve with the quadratic formula.

Step 1: Find the LCD
The denominators are \(x\) and \(x + 1\). They have no common factor, so
\[\text{LCD} = x(x+1)\]
Why: multiplying by the LCD cancels every denominator at once. Because \(x \ne 0\) and \(x \ne -1\), the LCD is not zero, so the multiplication is allowed.

Step 2: Multiply both sides by \(x(x+1)\)
\[x(x+1)\cdot\dfrac{1}{x} = x + 1\]
\[x(x+1)\cdot\dfrac{2}{x+1} = 2x\]
\[x(x+1)\cdot 1 = x(x+1)\]
So the equation becomes
\[(x+1) + 2x = x(x+1)\]
Why: each fraction loses its own denominator; the right side 1 must be multiplied too (every term on both sides).

Step 3: Expand and simplify
\[x + 1 + 2x = x^{2} + x\]
\[3x + 1 = x^{2} + x\]
Why: remove the brackets and collect like terms on each side.

Step 4: Write in standard form
\[x^{2} + x - 3x - 1 = 0\]
\[x^{2} - 2x - 1 = 0\]
Here \(a = 1\), \(b = -2\), \(c = -1\).
Why: the quadratic formula needs the equation in the form \(ax^{2} + bx + c = 0\); we moved \(3x + 1\) to the right side and wrote it as \(= 0\).

Step 5: Apply the quadratic formula
\[b^{2} - 4ac = (-2)^{2} - 4(1)(-1)\]
\[= 4 + 4 = 8\]
\[x = \dfrac{-(-2) \pm \sqrt{8}}{2(1)}\]
\[x = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{8}}{2}\]
Why: the discriminant 8 is not a perfect square, so \(x^{2} - 2x - 1\) does not factorise over whole numbers; the formula always works.

Step 6: Simplify the surd
\[\sqrt{8} = \sqrt{4 \cdot 2} = 2\sqrt{2}\]
\[x = \dfrac{2 \pm 2\sqrt{2}}{2}\]
\[x = 1 \pm \sqrt{2}\]
Why: take the perfect square 4 out of the root, then divide both terms of the numerator by 2.

Step 7: Compare with the restrictions
\(1 + \sqrt{2} \approx 2.414\) and \(1 - \sqrt{2} \approx -0.414\). Neither is \(0\) or \(-1\), so both are accepted.
Why: a value that makes a denominator zero would have to be rejected even though it came out of the quadratic.

Check:
For \(x = 1 + \sqrt{2}\) (rationalise each fraction):
\[\dfrac{1}{1+\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2} - 1\]
\[\dfrac{2}{2+\sqrt{2}} = 2 - \sqrt{2}\]
\[(\sqrt{2} - 1) + (2 - \sqrt{2}) = 1\]
For \(x = 1 - \sqrt{2}\):
\[\dfrac{1}{1-\sqrt{2}} = -1 - \sqrt{2}\]
\[\dfrac{2}{2-\sqrt{2}} = 2 + \sqrt{2}\]
\[(-1 - \sqrt{2}) + (2 + \sqrt{2}) = 1\]
Both values satisfy the original equation.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our own illustration of step 6 (not from the book): solve \(\frac{x^{2}}{x-2} = \frac{4}{x-2}\), \(x \ne 2\).
Multiplying by \(x - 2\): \(x^{2} = 4\), so \(x = 2\) or \(x = -2\).
But \(x = 2\) makes the denominator zero, so it is rejected. Solution set \(= \{-2\}\).
The quadratic gave two numbers, the equation has only one solution.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Start your answer by writing the restrictions (e.g. \(x \ne 0, x \ne -1\)) and finish with "Solution set \(= \{\dots\}\)". Examiners look for both. If the discriminant is not a perfect square, go straight to the quadratic formula instead of trying to factorise.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A rational equation has the variable in a denominator.
2. Values that make a denominator zero are excluded from the start.
3. Multiplying both sides by the LCD turns the equation into a quadratic.
4. Solve the quadratic, then reject excluded values and check in the original equation.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Multiplying only the fractions by the LCD and forgetting a whole-number term (like the 1 on the right of Example 7).
2. Sign slips in \(b^{2} - 4ac\): \(-4(1)(-1) = +4\).
3. Dividing only one term of \(2 \pm 2\sqrt{2}\) by 2; both terms must be divided.
4. Keeping a root that makes a denominator zero.
